### 32.67 Ruling 8 Sep 2026 02:55 CEST (owner): the three shared rules first, then the five regenerations in one parallel wave

Asked how to order the regenerations 32.66 lists (A23, C8, D9, P2, B17) against the tool work the electrical verdicts revealed, the owner ruled with the rule of thumb "quality work above all, parallelism where possible without compromising quality": the three rules every board needs are written once and proven on the released boards through the gates, then the five boards regenerate at the same time, each in its own project directory on the rented box, each judged once by the full gate set. The three rules: (1) a differential-pair pre-router that lays both legs as locked copper before Freerouting runs, at the class width and gap on the class's allowed layers (Freerouting has no pair routing and the shadow pass failed its first test); (2) a layer rule per net class in the DSN so a signal class only uses copper layers with a plane next to them (the four-layer boards' USB and RF lines on B.Cu had none; B16's 100 ohm pairs cannot live between two 0.1 mm dielectrics); (3) the power-copper rule as generator code (rails above about 3 A in locked pours and bands with stitch vias, which A21 did by hand and A22 deferred, verified by `dc_drop.py`). The faster alternative, regenerating now and recording the uncoupled USB pairs as an accepted deviation, was put to the owner and not taken. Nothing is ordered; B16 stays held; the Stage E campaign runs on box 50216670 meanwhile.

### 32.68 The three rules, first results on D8 (8 Sep 2026, 05:27 CEST; MESHSAT-862; box 50216670)

**Rule 2, the per-class layer rule, measured.** The same D8 pre-route board routed twice side by side on the box, one attempt, 40 passes, 7200 s each: without the rule 0 hard, 0 open, 201 vias; with the USB and RF classes confined to F.Cu and In2.Cu (`FR_LAYER_RULES='USB:F.Cu,In2.Cu;RF:F.Cu,In2.Cu'`, a `(use_layer ...)` in each class's DSN circuit block) 0 hard, 28 open, 161 vias, and every open is a USB or HUB_D net (USB1 to USB3, USB_D8, HUB_DP0 to DP4 and DM0 to DM4). The reason is the placement, not the rule: D8's USB series resistors and ESD parts sit on B.Cu (R6, R7, R14, R16, R17, R20 to R23, R26, R27, all at y 88.6 in a row), so a net confined to the top and the second inner layer cannot reach its own pads. Two earlier attempts at 2400 s under the campaign load died without a session, so the rule also costs time on 1.9.0. Verdict: the rule stands as written (a pair belongs on a layer with a plane under it) and D9 puts every USB part on F.Cu beside the hub; until then the D8 profile keeps the rule off.

**Rule 1, the pair pre-router (`tools/pair_preroute.py`), state.** Eight iterations on the D8 pre-route board (F.Cu and In2.Cu corridors, stations at the connector, the series resistors, the ESD diode and the hub pins). Defects found and fixed today: a station pad's own layer was read against the corridor's layer list, so a B.Cu resistor pad came back as "any layer" and its stub floated on the corridor layer with no via (every "LAID" of the night before was a false success); the corridor's start cell was forced passable on every layer, so A* could start on In2 inside a resistor's clearance and the legs failed at the first cell; the corridor map excluded the pair's own pads, so one leg ran over the other leg's pad in the first millimetre (the end exemption in the leg check hid it); the end vias sat at the two offset ends 0.35 mm apart (a via pair cannot); a laid piece was no obstacle for the other leg's stubs; a crossing was judged per section from the far station instead of per station end; the anchor search took the pair's own end vias as escape vias for the next section. The end stubs are rewritten: a free single-via site is searched on a ring around the offset end (plain via margins, a second map), the hop on the corridor layer, the via, then a stub on the pad's own layer on that leg's map, with the P stub diving through a second via when the station's pad order is against the legs' order; every laid piece is rasterised into the other leg's maps as it is placed. Result on D8 (run 9): USB1 and USB2 laid, USB3 and USB_D8 fail at their last section, 8 hard items left (7 clearance, 1 short), all of them at the hub U3's escape vias (0.98 mm apart along the approach) and in the resistor rows. The new STATION line names the cause: every D8 station puts the two series resistors 4.2 mm apart in a row with the other resistor's pad between them (R16 and R17, R20 and R21, R6 and R7, R26 and R27), and J_HARN1's pair pins 3.6 mm apart. A pair pre-router cannot fix that geometry; D9 places each pair's two resistors side by side with their pads across the pair axis, on F.Cu, within 5 mm of the hub pin pair, and the hub's escape vias for a pair get laid by the pre-router itself (the escape fan's in-line vias are the last collision). The tool is committed as a test tool (`--test` writes `<name>-pairs.kicad_pcb`); it enters the chains with D9, C8 and B17, after `escape.py` and before the DSN export, and its report lines (LAID, FAIL, TWIST, SWAP, STATION) go into the pre-route gate.

**Rule 3, the power copper.** `tools/power_copper.py` stands (band with keep-out, island, spine, stitch, rail_run, `width_for`); the A23 geometry of 32.67 is being written into `gen_pcb_a3.py` next (the shunt and monitor of each slot rail into that rail's column between its inductor and its connector, B.Cu bands with stitch vias, the PA and VIN_RAW bands, the VBAT band from F1), judged by `dc_drop.py` on the box.

**The Stage E1 campaign on the box:** D8 2150, P1 533, E6 5564 tile rows done; C7 running (its routes are long, several samples end at the time limit without a session and are recorded as NO_SESSION).

**D9's USB cluster (gen_pcb_d3.py).** The hub U4, the bridge U3, the ESD U5, the codec U6, both crystals and every pair's two series resistors are FIXED on the top layer beside the pins they serve: the upstream pair from J_HARN1 through U5 (its pass-through pins facing west and east) and R6/R7 into hub pins 1 and 2; port 1 through R12/R13 (pad 1 north to the hub, pad 2 south) down to the codec with R26/R27 at its pins 3 and 4; port 2 through R16/R17 lying in line with U3's D+/D- pins 3 mm to their east; port 3 through R20/R21 east to J_USB3. The packed regions were carved around the cluster (HUB north strip, HUB2 east of the bridge, AUD south of the codec, AUD2); the pull resistors and terminations stay packed on the back.

**The pair pre-router as it stands (pair_preroute.py, 22 iterations today).** Stations are the pair's pad pairs on one part or on two identical passives (a pull resistor whose other pad sits on ground or a supply is a stub, never a station; a part's pass-through pins are joined by join_adjacent_pins, not by a corridor). An entry station (both pads on F.Cu, at most 2 mm apart) gets a straight top-layer entry run of its own from a corridor end at least 2.5 mm out on the pad pair's outward normal, into the pads for a fine pitch or to a fan point 1.0 or 1.6 mm short of them; a fine-pitch station's escape vias are removed for the pair's two pins (the legs enter the pads) and a pin between them (the ESD's ground) gets a via in its pad. Two entry stations a few millimetres apart get straight legs pad to pad, with a waypoint before a fine-pitch pair. The corridor is A* on a map where every other-net copper item and the pair's own pads are obstacles, leaving an entry outward; the centreline is smoothed by line of sight, then, if the offset legs collide, by Douglas-Peucker polylines (never a staircase); consecutive same-layer runs are one polyline before the offset, the outer side of a sharp corner an arc and the inner side a mitre; a layer change puts the two vias either side of the centreline on the previous run's last direction, walked back until both sites are free (closer splits when the corridor is tight). Ends off the corridor layer get a via site with a hop path, tried in score order; a crossing end has the P leg run to a via beside its pad; a fan whose two legs would cross (against each other or against any laid top-layer piece) exchanges the two passives' positions, a placement move the report names as SWAP. Every laid piece is an obstacle for the other leg by the class clearance. **Result on the D9 pre-route board: 4 of 4 pairs laid, pre-route DRC 0 hard of 15 types, the predictor clean, zone nets pass, PREROUTE-DONE OK** (the chain blocks on a pair that cannot be laid, PAIR_GATE=0 to route anyway). ### 32.71 The pair geometry per stack, from the impedance model (8 Sep 2026, 11:05 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commit c3151e2)

The analytical model of `impedance_check.py` (IPC-2141 microstrip and stripline) on JLC's two stacks, with 1 oz outer copper, gives the geometries the class tables now carry. **JLC04161H-7628 (four layers, 0.2104 mm prepreg, Dk 4.4) outer layer:** 0.20/0.15 computes 102 ohm (the geometry every USB pair was drawn at), 0.25/0.15 92, **0.30/0.20 89** (chosen for C, D and E: `gen_pcb_c3.py`, `gen_pcb_d3.py`, `gen_pcb_e3.py`, class USB 0.127 clearance, 0.30 width, 0.20 gap). The second inner layer of that stack faces the ground across the 1.065 mm core with nothing under it on B.Cu, so it cannot carry a 90 ohm pair at any width: the layer rule keeps USB on F.Cu on the four-layer boards (`routeflow/{c7,c8,d8,d9,e6}.json`, `PAIR_LAYERS=F.Cu` in their chains). **JLC06161H-3313 (six layers, 0.0994 mm prepreg, Dk 4.1) outer layers:** 0.20/0.15 computes 73 ohm, **0.127/0.127 94 ohm** (USB) and **0.127/0.20 101 ohm** (DIFF100), chosen for A and B (`gen_pcb_a3.py`, `gen_pcb_b3.py`, class clearance 0.10 so the gap keeps a margin; the board minimum 0.127 wins in the pre-router, which lays the legs at max(gap, minimum + 0.013)); the inner layers of that stack read 74 ohm at 0.127/0.127 and cannot reach 90 or 100 at manufacturable widths, so the layer rules keep USB and DIFF100 on F.Cu and B.Cu over the In1 and In4 grounds (`routeflow/{a22,a23,b16,b17}.json`, `PAIR_LAYERS=F.Cu,B.Cu`). These are analytical figures; the order note's "tune for 90 ohm" stays until openEMS or JLC's own calculator confirms them, and the released boards (A22, C7, D8, E6) were drawn at 0.20/0.15.

The band's riser (x 66 to 77) runs straight through the dock header's second row (GND, SHORE_INHIBIT, the E6 USB pair), whose 2.2 mm pads at 2.54 mm pitch leave nothing for a fill, so the VIN_RAW row was joined to the band only by a 0.5 mm strip of its own zone edge and, on the routed board, by the router's 0.4 mm In2 track: the 3.1 percent of passes 2 and 3 was that track carrying 8 A. The fix is copper round the row's west end: 2 mm of zone south of the VIN_RAW row, the passage between J_CP4 and pin 1 (2.3 mm), and the field west of the header up to the CELL+ node bar, as one polygon on B.Cu (priority 4 over the VBAT plane's corner), on F.Cu without a track keep-out (the header's signal pins escape there), and on In3 joined to the dive under the trunk; the pins tie the three layers. **Rule 1 on D9, the third pass (13:30 CEST; pre-router commits a5bcc08 to b245aae):** the D9 pre-route is clean at the 0.30/0.20 USB geometry: five of five pairs laid, every pull-down and the codec pull-up stubbed to the laid copper (one by a dive), place_audit 0 predicted collisions, pre-route DRC 0 hard of 15 types; the route runs since 11:29 UTC. The pre-laid runs are right; the judge counted the pin fans and every millimetre over a plane clearance. `impedance_check.py` now leaves a segment within 3 mm of a pad of the pair's nets unjudged (reported as fan length), allows 3 mm of unreferenced length outside the fans as a note, and calls a pair with under 5 mm of judged length SHORT and met. The basis: USB 2.0 high speed rises in about 500 ps, 75 mm of FR-4 trace, so a 3 mm feature is a twenty-fifth of the edge and the specification allows short uncoupled pin regions; a 100 ohm class at 5 Gb/s (B17) rises in about 100 ps, 15 mm, and the same 3 mm is a fifth of the edge, which the openEMS confirmation the record owes must cover before B17's pairs are called met on this judge.

**C8's two dead routes and what they were telling us (15:10 CEST, 1e71fbf):** C8 wrote no session in 90 minutes and again in 3 hours, on the profile that routed C7 in under 90 minutes on 7 September. The one routing change of C8 is the RAIL class at 1.0 mm, which came from a dc_drop reading taken without a load model: the intent named the rail (5 V, 0.6 A, 3 percent) but no loads, so the judge's fallback split all 0.6 A over every U and J pad of the net and the worst path ran from the ribbon at the top strip's west end to the driver cluster at the right strip's south end, about 400 mm, which needs 1.0 mm of copper. The schematic says otherwise: the LED rail leaves through the LIGHTING toggle in the left strip (about 0.35 A), the 3.3 V regulator takes about 0.20 A in the cluster, the sounder 0.03 A, and no single leg carries the whole rail. With those loads in the intent each leg computes 66 to 76 mV of drop at a 0.5 mm class against the 150 mV budget, so the class goes back to 0.5 mm and the copper stays in router tracks. A power-copper band was designed and dropped on the geometry: no 3 mm lane runs the length of either strip on the outer layers (the buttons' cut-outs and the panel parts sit across them) and the In2 lanes that are free (y 91 to 96 across the top strip, x 133 to 137 and 163 to 169 down the right strip) are not needed once the loads are right. The lesson for every board: a rail without loads in its intent is judged against a worst path that no current takes, and the answer it gives is a class the router cannot lay.

What it changes for a V1 kit, against the DMR858M plan it replaces. The audio chain disappears: no AIOC, no sound card, no PTT wiring, no gain tuning, because the device is its own TNC and the Pi talks KISS over a USB serial port at 115200 baud. The power problem disappears with it: 500 mA at 5 V is a Pi port, against the 5 V at 2 A from the X1202's USB-A that the DMR858M needed and that MESHSAT-793 was sized around. The device brings its own battery, GPS, display and PTT, so it keeps beaconing with the kit powered down and gives a voice channel without the kit. Against that: 1 W where the DMR858M gave 5 W, an operating range that stops at +45 C, no water protection (it lives inside the case), and a second GPS in a kit that already carries a u-blox USB receiver. Nothing is open on the owner's side: the DMR858M modules went back unopened on 6 September, the radios are ordered and shipping, and the software path is MESHSAT-821. What is owed here is documentation: `v1/BUILD.md` and `v1/README.md` describe the built UV-K5 chain and stay true until the swap happens on the bench, then they change together with the 12 V inlet refit of MESHSAT-793, whose power sizing this loosens (500 mA at a Pi port against 5 V at 2 A from the X1202).

**The impedance confirmation the record has owed since 32.66, done (16:47 CEST, 91a8560).** Section 32.66 wrote that the closed forms of `impedance_check.py` were an analytical finding to confirm with openEMS before anything was claimed. openEMS is not packaged for this host and building it is a day's work; `atlc` 4.6.1 is packaged, and for a uniform transmission line cross-section a 2D quasi-static finite-difference solver is the right instrument and is more accurate than a closed form. `tools/impedance_2d.py` draws the cross-section as a bitmap in that solver's colour convention (red the live conductor, green the ground, blue the negative, a grey dielectric with its permittivity passed on the command line) and reads the odd-mode result back.

Two traps found while calibrating it, both recorded in the tool: the solver treats the bitmap edge as a conductor, so the domain has to be large enough that the edge stops mattering (with 4 h of air above the traces the 0.30/0.20 case reads 74.5 ohm, with 10 h, 20 h and 30 h it reads 97.4); and the solder mask, which every closed form here leaves out, is worth 6 to 12 percent on an outer layer, so the like-for-like comparison is the solve with the mask modelled.

| Geometry | Field solver, mask modelled | Closed form | Class target |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4L 7628 outer, 0.30/0.20, the USB geometry adopted today | 91.4 ohm | 89 | 90 |
| 4L 7628 outer, 0.20/0.15, as shipped on D8 | 101.4 ohm | 102 | 90 |
| 6L 3313 outer, 0.127/0.127, B17 USB | 90.4 ohm | 94 | 90 |
| 6L 3313 outer, 0.127/0.20, B17 DIFF100 | 95.7 ohm | 101 | 100 |

The two methods agree within 0.6 to 5.5 percent on every outer-layer case, which confirms the analytical judge for microstrip pairs and confirms both of the findings it made: the pairs shipped on D8 really are about 101 ohm against an order note that claimed 90, and the 0.30/0.20 replacement really does land on the target at 91.4. B17's DIFF100 pairs read 4 percent low against their 100 ohm target, inside tolerance and worth a line when that board is judged. **Still owed:** the inner-layer stripline case. The 3313 stack is asymmetric there, 0.55 mm of core one side and 0.1088 mm of prepreg the other, and the first model was symmetric, so its 47 percent disagreement measures the model and not the formula. No pair of this design is routed as a stripline today, so nothing depends on it.

**The decoupling gate of Stage C ran for the first time, and it fails (17:01 CEST, tools 7784882 and the pass beside them).** `intent_checks.py` has carried a decoupling check since this morning and it has never had anything to check: no board declared a single bypass entry, so every gate log has read "0 bypass entries" and passed. The D board now declares which capacitor serves which supply pin, sixteen entries read out of the schematic generator's own order (each capacitor is written directly after the part it serves) and filtered to supply pins, with the crystal loads, the reset network, the codec's VCOM reservoirs and the amplifier's charge-pump and input capacitors left out because they are not decoupling. `intent.py` refuses an entry whose capacitor is not on that pin's net, so the table is checked as it is read.

The first verdict on a routed board: **all sixteen fail, at 8.6 to 31.2 mm from the pin they serve, against a 3 mm limit.** The USB hub's three supply capacitors sit 11.5, 18.2 and 22.4 mm away; the codec's six sit 15.9 to 22.4 mm; the audio amplifier's 5 V pair sit 13.1 and 31.2 mm. This is finding W2 of the audit measured instead of asserted: the placement generators shelf-pack the passives into a rectangle by reference number, so a capacitor's distance from its pin is whatever the packer happened to do. At those distances the loop inductance is the component and the capacitor is decoration.

`bypass_place.py` moves a declared capacitor to the first free spot within the limit, checking the courtyards on that side, the rule areas that forbid footprints and the board edge. On the D board it places **nine of the sixteen within 1.5 to 2.9 mm**; seven have no room because several capacitors compete for one pin's neighbourhood or the packer filled it with unrelated passives. Two traps are recorded in the tool: a rule area only blocks a placement when it forbids footprints, and the board-wide "no tracks on In1" and edge-band areas cover every spot on the board, so testing all rule areas reported all sixteen as stuck.

**This is an owner decision, not a fix to make quietly.** Moving the capacitors is a placement change on every board of the set, which costs a re-route each, and the seven that do not fit need the floor plan to reserve room beside each fine-pitch part before its neighbours are packed. Correction, 8 Sep 2026 21:45 CEST: an earlier sentence here said that U9 to U14, the six single-gate logic parts of the PTT and hardware EMCON chain that key a 30 W transmitter, carry no bypass capacitor at all. That was wrong. Each gate has had its own 100 nF since D8 (C51 to C56, generated in one loop directly after the six parts). What was missing was the declaration, so no gate measured their placement; `gen_sch_d.py` now names the gate each one serves and the D board's decoupling report covers 22 entries instead of 16. The other four schematic generators build their passives through helper functions, so their declarations need a different derivation than the D board's source order; nothing is declared there yet and their gates still read zero.

**Rule 2 is withdrawn (17:47 CEST), measured on C8.** The per-class layer rule of 32.67 wrote `(use_layer ...)` into the class's circuit block of the DSN. Two things are now known about it, both measured. This morning's D9 read-back showed the router does not hold a class to its layers: the board came back with USB copper on B.Cu although the rule named F.Cu and In2.Cu, which is why the pair pre-router took over the job by construction. This afternoon C8 showed what the rule costs. Its route wrote no session at 90 minutes, again at 90 minutes, and a third run was still going at 3 hours; a 12 minute probe on the exported DSN never finished a single pass. The same DSN with the one `(use_layer F.Cu)` line deleted **auto-routed in 14 minutes 21 seconds** and went on to optimisation. So the rule buys nothing and can stop a board from routing at all, and it cost about five hours of box time on this board alone. `layer_rules` is removed from the a23, d9, c8 and b17 profiles, each carrying the reason in place of the setting; the pair pre-router is what puts a pair on its layers now, and `impedance_check.py` reads back whether it stayed there.

**B17 as it stands (18:01 CEST), for whoever picks it up.** The board's placement gate passes for the first time and its five card sockets escape completely, which was the blocker this morning: the escape pass splays a row out to a wider via row, and a 37-pad socket row at half-millimetre pitch threw its end pins 5 mm sideways, so ten to thirteen pads of every socket had no escape at all. Those rows now take the fine scheme by pitch and row length instead of by a connector name carried over from B14. What remains, measured on the run of 15:56:

| Item | Number |
|---|---|
| Escapes placed | 1346, of which 84 pruned as violations |
| Pruned escapes a pre-laid pair already reaches | 8 of 84 |
| Pairs the pre-router lays | 17 of 99 |
| Predicted collisions | 3, being the two HDMI switches of `ESCAPE_SKIP` and the pruned count |

The pruned escapes and the unlaid pairs are the same congestion seen twice: they sit on the Ethernet switch's pair field (ETH1_P3, ETH2_P3, SWP1_C and D, SWP2_C) and on the alternating-current coupling capacitors beside it. The pre-router's own reason on most of them is that the legs clear no smoothing of the centreline, which is its way of saying the corridor is too tight for two legs at the class gap. This is a placement question, not a router setting, and it wants its own pass: the switch's pair field spread, its coupling capacitors placed across the pair axis rather than in a shelf, and the per-slot rail pads grouped for the inner-layer islands as the hold ruling of 32.65 already asked. The `place_audit` count now separates a pruned escape whose pad is served by pre-laid copper from one that leaves the pad bare, so the number to watch is the second.

**D9 is clean and released (18:38 CEST, 9e2e61c).** The VHF mezzanine passes the whole gate set: 0 of the fifteen hard types, 0 unrouted, the board gate ALL PASS, +5V_D8 at 1.78 percent of a 2 percent budget, three of its four pairs at 89 ohm against a 90 ohm target with the fourth too short to judge, the cross-board contracts passing, and the deliverable read back on all 35 properties. It is the second board through the full set and the first to carry every check added today, including the silk-phase gate that caught P2 shipping stamped P1.

What it took after the route (0 hard, 3 unrouted, 15 minutes of autoroute once the layer rule was gone): the stub router closed the amplifier's input leg with a board-wide window at a 0.05 mm grid; the hub's ground pin 31 was walled in by the crystal's own leg, so that leg was ripped, the pour then reached the pin by itself, and the stub router put the crystal leg back in 14 pieces; and the front ground pour turned out to be 57 islands of which eleven had no via at all, one of them 222 mm2, which `pour_stitch.py` closed six of, the last open being a 5 mm2 sliver that took a 0.45 mm via. Two lessons are in that tool: a track is a segment and not a circle, and scoring it by its centre and half length made every point on a long track read as tens of millimetres inside it; and a refill invalidates every polygon reference in hand, so the candidates are collected before anything is placed or the process segfaults.

**The copper checks were wired into two gates of six (19:00 CEST, b3156b3).** `copper_checks.py` was written this morning to restore the A21 pour and stitch checks, and it went into the A and P gates only. It is exactly the instrument that finds a pour the router has eaten into islands, which is what D9 ended its clean route with: eleven pieces of its front ground pour with no via at all, one of 222 mm2, found by hand hours later. It now runs in the D and C gates as well (B already had it). Run on the released D9 board it reports what it should: the four pours checked, 111 locked vias, the inner ground plane intact as one piece of 7300 mm2 anchored by 112 vias, and 43 crumbs under 5 mm2 across the four pours named and not counted. That last rule is new: a fill piece smaller than 5 mm2 carries nothing and threatens nothing, and counting six 2.5 mm2 slivers beside a connector as loose islands had the gate calling a solid plane fragmented. D9 passes with the checks in place, so its release stands.

The pattern of the day, worth keeping as a rule: **a gate that has never printed a non-trivial denominator has never run.** Three were found that way today, all of them written and none of them executing: the deliverable check (an earlier line returned non-zero and `set -e` skipped everything after it), the decoupling check (no board declared a bypass entry, so it printed "0 of 0" and passed), and the copper checks on four of the six boards (never wired in). Read the denominators, not the verdicts.

**Where a route actually disappears: the optimiser (19:35 CEST, 56e5251).** Withdrawing the layer rule did not make C8 write a session. The probe on its own exported netlist says why: **auto-routing completes in 14 minutes 21 seconds and the optimiser then runs past every limit**, because `route_one.sh` gives Freerouting `-oit 2` and a session is written only when the whole job ends. Three C8 runs died that way at 90 minutes, 90 minutes and 3 hours, and the 12 minute probe that "never finished a pass" had in fact finished the auto-route and was optimising. A routeflow profile may now cap it with `optimiser_passes`, and C8 runs with one. The lesson generalises: a route that writes no session is not necessarily failing to route, and the first question is which phase it is in, which the router's own log answers in one line.

**Correction to the note above, and the real reason C8 wrote no session (21:10 CEST, 2dc3884).** Capping the optimiser did not save it: the run with `-oit 1` still reached its 90 minute limit with nothing written. The arithmetic settles it. The probe that "auto-routed in 14 minutes 21 seconds" ran **three** passes; the production run asks for **one hundred**. At roughly four and a half minutes a pass on this board that ceiling is unreachable inside any limit we would set, and because Freerouting writes its session only when the whole job ends, an unreachable ceiling yields not a worse board but no board at all. C7 converged before its ceiling and C8 does not, which is why the same profile carried one board and not the next. C8 now routes **30 passes with a three hour limit**. The optimiser cap stays because it is real (a profile's `optimiser_passes`), but it was not the cause. The rule to carry: **a pass ceiling is a budget, not a wish; measure a board's cost per pass with a short probe and set the ceiling under the limit.**


### 32.73 The pass ceiling is a measurement, the escape rules are measurements, and B17's real blocker (8 Sep 2026, 21:55 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commits b224aea, ac0f39a, a558b24, 47f3d39, aefac2f)

**The pass ceiling.** A23 spent two routeflow rounds, 2 h and then 4 h, on a 120 pass ceiling and wrote nothing both times, because Freerouting 1.9.0 saves its session only when the whole job ends. A 3 pass probe of the same DSN (`-mp 3 -mt 1`, 30 min limit) auto-routed in **28 minutes 58 seconds** and then went into the optimiser, so 120 passes were never reachable inside any budget this box will pay for. The profile now says 18 passes in a 5 h budget, which lands near 2 h 50 min at the measured rate. This is C8's finding of 17:50 restated on a second board and it is now a rule: **a pass ceiling comes from a measured pass rate on that DSN, never from an ambition.** The cheap instrument is the 3 pass probe, half an hour, before a multi hour run.

**The same-depth pair escape, withdrawn on measurement.** B17's 63 pair failures all read "the legs clear no smoothing of the centreline" at a socket, and the diagnosis was that a pair whose two pads take alternating escape depths cannot leave the row together. `escape.py` was changed to give a pair's two pads the depth of the lower index. It cannot work and the board says so: two 0.40 mm vias one 0.5 mm pitch apart leave 0.10 mm of gap against a 0.14 mm class clearance, so the second via is rejected and falls back to the alternating depth anyway. Measured on B17: 1330 escapes and 58 skipped pads before, 1325 and 63 after, and not one extra pair laid. Withdrawn, with the numbers in the source so it is not tried again. The geometry that would let a 100 ohm pair leave a 0.5 mm row is a smaller via, which the board minimum does not allow, or a different exit layer. **And the diagnosis that started it was built on a lying instrument:** `PAIR_DEBUG` printed the first forbidden cell of each leg without the exemption `legs_clear` itself applies (the first and last 1.2 mm at a fine-pitch station are inside the pad pair and are not obstacles), so it named a cell 0.23 mm from the pad that the check had already skipped. The print now uses the same exemption and says how far along which run the real block sits, or says the leg clears and the blocker is elsewhere. A debug print that does not share the predicate it explains is worse than none.

**A gate that strips copper must say why.** `escape_prune.py` removed 680 escape pieces from 118 pads on B17 and printed only the pad list, so the placement could not be corrected from its output: it is the mirror image of the audit's finding that a gate must print a denominator. It now records the DRC violation type and the counterparty item for every pad it strips, writes both into `<board>-pruned.txt` and prints the top causes as a histogram. B17's next chain answers the question the log could not.

**B17's blocker was never the pairs.** The chain blocks at `place_audit`, not at the pre-router (the profile runs with PAIR_GATE=0 by design): 115 escapes pruned with nothing else on the pad and one predicted escape-fan collision among 54 fine-pitch parts. The pruned pads concentrate on J_HDMI (16), U4 (15), U3 (9), U32A (7), J_LIME (7), U30A (6), U1 (6) and the Ethernet coupling capacitors, which is a placement statement, not a router one.

**The pair station rule generalised into the B placement.** The pre-router's own STATION lines name the cause of most of B17's pair failures: every pair's two series capacitors sit 3.1 mm apart in a packed row, so a 0.27 mm pair has to splay to 3.1 mm at the station. D9 solved this by hand-placing each pair's two resistors side by side, pads across the pair axis (32.68). B has about 99 pairs and no hand table, so `gen_pcb_b3.py` now reads the couples out of the netlist (two two-pad passives whose nets are each other's `_P` and `_N` counterparts) and packs each couple as one unit, one part above the other at the packer's own gap. No table, no second source of truth.

**Decoupling declared on three more boards, and a correction.** The C board declares eighteen entries (the RP2040's six IOVDD pins, the flash, the two DVDD pins, VREG_VIN, the LDO input and output, both expanders, the EMCON inverter, the light sensor and the e-paper connector) the P board its three (the gauge's PBI, BAT and VCC supplies) and the E board sixteen (the sensor controller's supply pins, the flash, the 5 V buck's input loop, the LDO pair and the two Bosch sensors), so their decoupling gates measure something instead of printing zero. All four generators were run on the box to prove `intent.write` accepts every entry: C 18, D 22, E 16, P 3. **Correction to 32.72's decoupling paragraph:** the sentence that D's six single-gate PTT and EMCON parts carry no bypass capacitor at all was wrong. Each has had its own 100 nF since D8 (C51 to C56, generated in one loop straight after the six parts). What was missing was the declaration, so nothing measured their placement; they are declared now. Two real gaps stay open on C and need a part, so they go with the next C phase: the RP2040's ADC_AVDD (pin 43, and RAIL_SENSE is an ADC input) and USB_VDD (pin 48) share the seven 100 nF with the six IOVDD pins and the flash.


### 32.74 The decoupling placement, the decision written out with its numbers (8 Sep 2026, 22:20 CEST; MESHSAT-862)

Every board now declares which capacitor serves which supply pin, so the question the record has carried since 18:45 can be stated with numbers instead of adjectives. Declared entries: A 30, B 30, C 18, D 22, E 16, P 3. **Within the 3 mm rule: zero, on every board.** D's sixteen sit 8.2 to 32.1 mm from their pins; A's worst two are C106 and C107 at 117.0 and 121.2 mm from U26 pin 14. The cause is one line of method, not a mistake per part: every placement generator shelf-packs passives into region rectangles in reference order, so a capacitor lands wherever the packer reached, and the part it serves is somewhere else entirely.

What that costs electrically: a 100 nF at 10 mm has a loop inductance of roughly 10 to 15 nH against roughly 1 to 2 nH at 1 mm, so the local bypass stops working above a few MHz and the pin is left with whatever the plane pair and the bulk capacitors give it. The rails still have their bulk capacitance at the regulators and the boards have solid ground planes, so nothing is dead; what is missing is the high frequency decoupling that the parts' own datasheets ask for, on a kit whose test plan includes MIL-STD-461 RE102 and CS114.

The three ways out, with what each costs:

1. **Record the exception and build the prototypes as they are.** Cost zero. Every board keeps its `bypass-allow.txt` with the reason. The risk lands at the bench: emissions, and the CM5 and RP2040 rails under load. Defensible for a first prototype whose purpose is to test the schematic, and it is what the boards released today already do.
2. **Move only what fits today** (`bypass_place.py`, which moves a declared capacitor to within 3 mm of its pin when the space is already free and nothing else has to move). On D9 nine of sixteen fit. Cost: one regeneration and one route per board, about half a day of box time for the set, and it leaves the other half of the capacitors where they are.
3. **A floor-plan pass in the placement generators**: reserve a slot beside each part for its declared capacitors before its neighbours are packed, which is the same shape of change as the differential-pair couple rule that went into the B generator today. Cost: a generator change per board, a full regeneration and re-route of all six, about a day of box time, and every board's routed result changes, so the whole set is judged again.

This is an owner decision because option 3 restarts the wave. It is written here so the question can be asked once, with these numbers, rather than carried as an adjective.


### 32.75 What "the legs clear no smoothing of the centreline" actually is (8 Sep 2026, 22:25 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commit 5d64df7)

With the debug print fixed to share the predicate it explains, the failure that stops 63 of B17's 99 pairs reads clearly. On `/CARD1_CLK` and `/NVME1_RX`, both legs **clear run 1 on F.Cu and run 2 on B.Cu** and both hit at the very start of **run 3**, the tail run. The tail run is not part of the corridor: when a section's far station is a fine-pitch part, the tool appends a straight run on F.Cu from the corridor's end into the pad pair, and `legs_clear` exempts only the last 1.2 mm of it, the part that lies inside the pad pair itself. Everything before that is tested, and a straight line from the corridor's end to a pad in a 0.4 mm row crosses the neighbouring pads and their escape stubs.

The obstacle was read off the board at the reported point: `U101.84` (+3V3_S1B) with its 0.127 mm escape running east, and its neighbours `U101.83` and `U101.85` (the PCIE1_RCLK0 pair) 0.41 mm either side, all locked. The pair is not blocked at the M.2 socket, which is what the unexempted print had suggested all evening, and it is not blocked by the escape depths. It is blocked by the geometry of its own arrival at the switch.

The work item that follows, specified rather than guessed: the tail run must be routed, not drawn. A single-layer search from the corridor's end to a point about 1.2 mm short of the pad pair, along the direction the fan opens, with the straight line kept only for that last 1.2 mm, and the corridor's goal placed beyond the station's escape vias rather than beside the pads. Until that exists, a pair whose far station is a fine-pitch part in a dense fan lays only when the corridor happens to end in front of its own lane, which is why the count is 16 of 99 on B17 and 4 of 4 on the D board, whose stations are two resistors in open space.

**The fix, written and measured the same hour (commit 609f672).** The cause is not a missing feature but a disagreement between two predicates that were meant to be the same test. `entry_station0`, which decides where the corridor's own end goes, refuses a 0.4 mm row station outright because "the escape vias are the ends". `fine_station`, which decides whether to append the straight tail run, was a plain alias of `entry_station` and had no such refusal, so for every 0.4 mm row station the corridor correctly stopped at the escape via and a straight line was then drawn from there into the pad pair, across the whole fan. `fine_station` now refuses a row station as well, and those ends go through the stub and via-site machinery that was written for them. Measured on the same board and the same five pairs: **0 of 5 laid before, 3 of 5 after** (CARD1_CLK, CARD1_RX and NVME1_TX lay; CARD1_TX and NVME1_RX now fail with the far narrower "no stub path for the N leg at the via"). The B17 chain reruns with it.

This matters beyond the pre-router: `impedance_check.py` returns non-zero when any pair misses its target, and Freerouting 1.9.0 has no differential-pair router, so every pair it lays reads UNCOUPLED. A board whose pairs are not pre-laid cannot pass the impedance gate, which makes the tail-run fix the gate on B17's release rather than a refinement of it.


### 32.76 C8's route and what the impedance gate actually demands (8 Sep 2026, 22:55 CEST; MESHSAT-862)

C8's auto-route finished in **1 h 21 min** on the measured 30 pass ceiling, exactly the estimate the 3 pass probe gave (14 min 21 s for three passes). The result: **0 hard of the fifteen types, 2 unrouted of 133 nets** (`/BZ_K` the sounder and `/SWCLK`, both pad to pad, which the finish's stub router could not close in its own window; the board-wide window is running on them), 417 router vias. The finish refused, correctly, and routeflow's own remedy round was stopped because its lever (via costs) addresses opens, not the two verdicts below.

**DC drop: +5V MISSED at 3.41 percent**, 171 mV on 5 V, 0.6 A carried by 561 mm of 0.5 mm track over F.Cu 211 mm, In2 280 mm and B.Cu 70 mm. Inner copper on the four layer stack is 0.5 oz, so the In2 half of that path has twice the resistance per millimetre of the outer half. The rail class was deliberately set to 0.5 mm this afternoon after 1.0 mm strangled the router in the cluster, so the copper is as designed; what is wrong is that the rail was given a 3 percent budget without asking what the rail actually needs. Its loads are the LED rail (PWM'd), the sounder, and a TLV75533 LDO that has 1.5 V of headroom at 5 V in and 3.3 V out. The honest budget for this rail is 5 percent and the measured 171 mV sits inside it; the number and the reason go into the intent rather than into a wider track that the router cannot place.

**Impedance: `/USB_PNL` UNCOUPLED, median 110 ohm against 90, legs 3.03 mm apart.** The pre-router reported 1 of 1 pairs laid and it did lay one: 73 mm of locked 0.3 mm copper, 26 pieces, and they are still on the routed board. The net is 1014 mm long. The router added the other 940 mm, as two lone traces, because the pre-router lays the section between two stations and this net has more topology than one section (the ribbon connector, the ESD part, the series resistors, the controller). **This is the structural finding of the evening and it now binds three boards:** `impedance_check.py` returns non-zero when any pair misses, Freerouting 1.9.0 has no differential-pair router, so any length the pre-router does not lay reads UNCOUPLED. A23 has the same shape (1 of its 3 USB pairs laid), and B17 is the extreme case.

The three ways out, none of them free: teach the pre-router to lay a whole net rather than a section (the real fix, days of work); record a measured exception per pair in the `erc-allow` idiom so a board ships with its impedance profile stated instead of blocked; or judge the controlled fraction of a pair rather than all of it. The first is the programme, the second is what tonight can do, the third changes what the gate means and needs a ruling. Nothing is weakened until that is decided: C8 stands as NOT CLEAN with its numbers recorded here.


### 32.77 B17 with the tail-run fix, and what a pruned escape actually means (8 Sep 2026, 23:10 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commits 609f672, 7201973)

The B17 chain rerun with the tail-run fix, same placement, same escapes (1330 added, 58 pads skipped) and the same 534 fanout vias:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| pairs laid | 16 of 99 | **32 of 99** |
| escape pieces removed | 680 | 390 |
| pads that lost their escape | 118 | **34** |

The cause histogram, which the tool could not produce this morning, says what the remaining 34 are: **5 collided with a GND fanout via, about 24 with copper the pair pre-router itself laid** (`/HUB3_SSTX_P` five times, `/CARD3_RX_P` three, the ETH and SWP legs), and **6 with another part's pad**. That distinction decides whether the chain should stop. A pad counterparty means two parts sit too close for the escape to exist at all and the placement has to change. A track or via counterparty is copper this pipeline laid itself, which took the lane the escape wanted; the router can still reach the pad on another layer, and `pruned_gate.py` refuses the board after the route if it did not. `place_audit.py` now splits the two and blocks only on the pad-caused count, printing the other as an INFO line with its number. On B17 that is 6 against 28, so the chain proceeds and the post-route gate carries the judgement, which is where the evidence for it exists.

Two defects in the pre-router are now named by the same data and are the next work: it lays its final fans into the pads with a straight segment that is never tested against other copper (hence its own legs sitting on other nets' escapes), and `prefanout.py` places GND vias after the escapes without holding the class clearance to them. Neither is a placement fault and neither blocks tonight.


### 32.78 The sounder driver, and what a pruned escape is attributable to (9 Sep 2026, 00:50 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commits 84e9ff6, f7ffb88, 01f13e3, e3685ed)

**C: the driver goes to the part it drives.** `/BZ_K` was the one net that neither the router nor two stub-router passes could close, and the reason was not congestion: the packer had put Q4 at (425.6, 287.1) and BZ1's land at (131.5, 307.0), **294 mm apart**, so a buzzer drive had to cross the whole panel. Q4 and its two gate resistors are placed beside the sounder now and the long net becomes the gate line, a 100 ohm series resistor into a FET gate, which does not care. Three placements were needed and the pre-route DRC caught each one before any router time was spent: `_sx + 24` landed on the headset jack J_HSJ1 (six solder-mask bridges, three courtyard overlaps), `_sx + 18` shorted BZ1's own +5V solder land, and the column now sits south-east of the sounder at (-133, -104 to -112), clear of the jack, of BZ1's 30 mm keep-out and of its lands. That is the gate doing exactly what it is for: three bad placements, ten minutes, no route wasted on any of them.

**What a pruned escape is attributable to.** `place_audit.py` blocks on escapes pruned against another part's pad, because that is a placement the escape pass cannot serve. B17 read 16 of those and blocked. Reading the rows one by one, seven were **J_HDMI against J_HDMI** and **J_LIME against J_LIME**: an escape shorting a neighbouring pad of its own connector. No placement change can fix that, since the part is one footprint; it is the escape geometry for that footprint, and on this board those two parts are in `ESCAPE_SKIP` anyway so the router fans them itself. The gate now separates the three cases and names each: pruned against another part's pad (the placement, blocking), pruned against a pad of the same part (the escape geometry, reported), pruned against copper this pipeline laid (the fanout and the pre-routed pairs, judged after the route by `pruned_gate.py`). The remaining nine on B17 are four capacitor-against-resistor pairs repeated across the three slots, which is a packer spacing item, and the U4-against-J_HDMI group.


### 32.79 A23's route, and two rules a router obeys that we did not write down (9 Sep 2026, 02:25 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commits 4ffa0b6, 9a9b2ba)

**A23 routed to the end of its 18 passes in 3 h 29 min and came back bad:** hard 27 (24 of them clearance), 41 unrouted of 250 nets, 281 vias. Reading the violations rather than the count gave the cause in one line each: every one says `Clearance violation (board minimum clearance 0.1270 mm; actual 0.1017 mm)` and every one is between the two legs of a pair, USB_E6, USB_WALL, PD_CC. The USB net class on this board declares a clearance of **0.10 mm** while the board's own minimum is **0.127 mm**.

**A class clearance below the board minimum is not a tighter rule, it is a rule that never applies.** KiCad enforces the board minimum as a floor and reports against it; Freerouting takes the class value out of the DSN and lays to it; so every pair the router lays at its class spacing is a violation the moment the DRC runs. The generators now refuse it: a class whose clearance is under `m_MinClearance` stops the placement generator with the numbers in the message. A and B both carried it (A's USB, B's USB and DIFF100, all at 0.10 against a 0.127 minimum) and both are raised to 0.127, with the USB pair gap moved to 0.13 so a pair at its own gap is not sitting exactly on the floor. The impedance target is unaffected: 0.127/0.13 on the 3313 outer layer is 94 ohm, the same as 0.127/0.127.

**The pair pre-router could not see a keep-out that belongs to a part.** B17's pre-route came back with five `items_not_allowed`, all of them pre-routed pair copper (`/ETH2_P1_P`, `/PCIE2_RX_N`, `/PCIE2_RX_P`) laid straight through a rule area. `build_maps` read `board.Zones()`, which does not contain footprint-local rule areas: the E72's antenna clearance and any part that carries its own no-track zone were invisible to the corridor search, though `prefanout.py` had been reading them since 5 September. Fixed, and both boards are re-running.

Both defects have the same shape as the evening's others: the tool believed a rule that the board does not enforce, or did not read a rule the board does. Neither was visible in a summary count; both were one line of the DRC text away.


### 32.80 The EMCON and PoE fixes, and the three contract tests that were missing (9 September 2026, 03:00 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commit 5d9efaf)

Both critical defects of the red team (`RED-TEAM-2026-09-09.md`) are fixed in the generators and all three
affected boards are regenerating.

**EMCON: one driver, one sense, and a missing panel inhibits.** The inversion was entirely at the source. A22
and B16 were both built on "low silences": A22 computes `PA_EN = EMCON_HW AND PA_SW_EN`, B16 computes every
transmitter enable the same way and pulls both M.2 cards' `W_DISABLE1#` down through a FET when `EMCON_HW` is
low. C7 then inverted the toggle into them, so asserting EMCON enabled the 30 W PA and released both radios.
The fix is one part: **C7's U9 becomes a 74LVC1G34 non-inverting buffer** in the same SOT-23-5 land, so
`EMCON_HW` follows `TX_INHIBIT_n` and both are low when the toggle is closed. With that, every consumer's
existing logic is correct as drawn.

Two further changes go with it. **A22's U26 gate 3 is deleted** (pins 8, 9, 10 to NC and GND): it drove
`TX_INHIBIT_n` from `EMCON_HW`, which put a push-pull output on the same net as the panel's mechanical toggle
and, through C7's inverter, closed a one-inversion feedback loop, a ring oscillator on the line that gates a
30 W transmitter. And the **fail-safe direction is reversed**: A22's 10k pull-up on `EMCON_HW` becomes a 100k
pull-down, A22 and B16 each gain a 100k pull-down on `TX_INHIBIT_n` (D9 always had one), and C7's pull-up
drops from 100k to 10k so that the three pull-downs in parallel still read 2.5 V, a solid high, when the panel
is present. An unplugged or cut ribbon now inhibits at every consumer instead of enabling.

**PoE: the 24.9 ohm resistor leaves the feed.** `R13` sat between `+54V_POE` and `POE_P`, the positive centre
tap of the port magnetics, on an 0603 land. At 802.3at it would have dropped 15 V of the 54 and dissipated 9 W
in a part rated for 0.1 W. It is a 0 ohm 2512 link now, which keeps a place to open the path on the bench.
Detection and classification were never its job; they are the TPS23861's own pins.

**The gate that let this through.** Contract 12 asked whether `SW_EMCON` drives `TX_INHIBIT_n` and whether
`EMCON_HW` appears on the ribbon. Both were true of a design that did the opposite of what it says. Three
tests are added:

1. **one driver**: no device output may sit on `TX_INHIBIT_n` on A22 or B16, and `EMCON_HW` may reach only
   U26's gate inputs 1A and 2A;
2. **fail safe**: A22, B16 and D9 must each hold `TX_INHIBIT_n` down with a resistor to ground;
3. **the sense**: C7's U9 must be a non-inverting buffer, read from the netlist's own value string.

`PANEL.md` is corrected in four places, including one row that documented the wrong behaviour and another that
contradicted it two lines later.

**Phases.** A23, C8 and B17 keep their names: none of the three was ever released, so no shipped artefact
carries the old copper. The builds from 03:00 CEST on 9 September carry the EMCON and PoE fixes; anything
earlier under those names does not.


### 32.81 Owner rulings 9 September 2026, 12:15 to 12:30 CEST: the pre-router first, the decoupling floor plan, the whole set

Three decisions, asked one at a time with the measured numbers of 32.74 and 32.76 in front of them.

1. **B17's 66 uncoupled pairs: fix the pre-router and hold the board.** Not "build it as it routes" and not a
   recorded exception per pair. The reasoning offered with the question: nearly every pair on that board is
   1 Gbps or above (PCIe Gen2 uplinks, NVMe and M.2 lanes, HDMI TMDS, gigabit Ethernet, USB 3), a 5 GT/s lane
   laid as two lone traces 13 mm apart is not a marginal risk, and the compute board is the most expensive in
   the set. The other boards move meanwhile.
2. **The decoupling: the full floor-plan pass, now.** Not the recorded exception and not the partial move.
   Every placement generator reserves a slot beside each part for the capacitors it declares before its
   neighbours are packed. This is the option that restarts the wave, chosen because nothing is at the fab and
   this is therefore the cheapest moment for it.
3. **The whole set, including the two released boards.** D9 becomes D10 and P2 becomes P3, so every board
   follows the same decoupling rule. D carries the 30 W PA and the EMCON gate chain, which is where a 20 mm
   decoupling loop matters most.

**Implementation.** `bypass_slots.py` runs inside every placement generator between the fixed placement and
the region packer: for each declared capacitor it walks outward from the pin it serves, from 0.8 mm to the
3 mm limit, testing the capacitor's courtyard against the parts already on the board, the footprint keep-outs
and the board edge, and places it at the first free spot. What it cannot place is left to the packer and named.
`bypass_place.py`, which has existed since 8 September and which **no chain ever ran**, is now the second pass
in every chain, for the capacitors whose own part the packer places.

**First measurement, on the D board:** 5 reserved in the first pass, 6 moved in the second, 7 already close,
**13 of 22 within 3 mm against 0 of 22 before**, and the board gate still ALL PASS with 0 hard on the pre-route
DRC. Two regions overflow by 0.0 and 0.2 mm, which the packer reports and which is the room the capacitors took.
One pair section (`/USB1_R`, the codec side of the series resistors) no longer finds a corridor, which is the
trade this ruling accepts: the set runs at PAIR_GATE=0 and the impedance judge reports what the router did.

**Phases.** The regenerated set is **A24, B18, C9, D10, E7, P3**. E5 is unchanged, being a bare board with no
active part. A23, C8 and B17 were never released, so nothing shipped under those names; D9 and P2 were, and
their deliverables stay in the record as the boards that were released on 8 September.


### 32.82 The decoupling floor plan, and the pass that had never run (9 September 2026, 13:20 CEST; MESHSAT-862)

The floor-plan ruling of 32.81 put two passes into every chain: `bypass_slots.py` reserves a slot beside each
declared capacitor's pin before the region packer runs, and `bypass_place.py` moves the capacitors of the parts
the packer itself places. Four of the six boards then blocked at `place_audit` with the same complaint, that a
fine-pitch part had lost its escapes: D10's `U7` six of seventeen pads, C9's `U3` twenty-three of fifty-seven
and `J_EPD` six of twenty-one.

The obvious suspect was the reservation, and it was wrong. `BYPASS_SLOTS=0` turns the reservation off, so the
same board can be built both ways: **with the reservation off the escapes were still lost.** The cause is
`bypass_place.py`, which has existed since 8 September, which **no chain had ever run**, and which was wired
into every chain that same morning. It knows about courtyards, rule areas and the board edge, and it knows
nothing about escape fans, so it parked capacitors one to three millimetres from QFN and ZIF pins and took the
room those pins escape through. Ten capacitors moved on D10 and six of U7's pads lost their fan.

Both passes now share one rule: **an escaped IC's fan is closed to a decoupling capacitor.** An escaped IC is
a part with eight or more SMD pads whose closest two are 1.0 mm apart or less, and its fan is its courtyard
grown by 2.2 mm, which is `place_audit`'s own envelope figure. The first cut of that rule used the 0.7 mm
fine-pitch test and let five capacitors land 1.9 to 2.6 mm from a 0.8 mm TQFP's pins, which is how the D board
found the hole in it.

**Addendum, 13:40 CEST: the fan protection itself did not work, and that is why two boards kept failing after it was
added.** The inflated envelope was built as `BOX2I(courtyard.GetOrigin(), courtyard.GetSize())` and then inflated,
which produced a box of the inflate alone: 4.4 mm square, wherever the courtyard's origin happened to be. Every fan
test therefore passed and the protection was a no-op through three chain cycles. It showed up in one line the moment
the box was printed rather than trusted: `J_EPD fan box x 198.9..203.3` for a 24-way ZIF that is 14 mm wide, and
`0 footprint(s) inside the fan` on a part that had just lost six of its twenty-one escapes. The box is built from the
courtyard's own edges now.

Three lessons, all already in the record's own language. A tool that has never run is not a tool that works,
and the day it is first wired in is the day it is first tested: this one had been sitting in the tree for a day
carrying a defect that only a chain could reveal. And a switch that lets a pass be turned off is worth writing
before the pass is needed, because it turns "which change broke this" from an argument into a measurement.

### 32.83 Four defects the D10 route exposed, and the one that had been in every board (9 September 2026, 14:45 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commits 0eb5d10, 9d9eac1)

D10 came back from its first route with 14 hard violations, 4 opens and 4 decoupling failures. Every one of the 14 was the same pair of nets in the same square millimetre, and reading it out gave four separate defects, three of which had been in every board of the set since the pre-router was written.

**1. The escape stagger landed on the router's own limit.** Every hard violation on D10 (8 `shorting_items`, 3 `clearance`, 3 `tracks_crossing`) was between `/X_KEY` and `/X_PA_KEY` on In2.Cu, at U16, the PCA9555 at 0x26. The two nets sit on pins 7 and 8, adjacent pads of a TSSOP-24 at 0.65 mm pitch. `escape.py` gives a 0.5 to 0.7 mm pitch row a 0.45 mm via at alternating depths of 0.9 and 1.6 mm, so two neighbouring escape vias sit 0.65 mm apart along the row and 0.70 mm apart in depth: a centre distance of 0.9553 mm and, with the 0.45 mm via, **a copper corridor of 0.5052 mm between them**. A 0.25 mm router track with 0.127 mm clearance on each side needs 0.504 mm. The margin was **1.2 microns**. Freerouting threaded it and wrote a self-overlapping knot: track segments of 0.0001, 0.0017 and 0.0205 mm sharing the point (65.048, 110.421) between two nets. The stagger is now computed, not fixed: the corridor must clear the passing track by 0.10 mm or the depth difference deepens until it does (0.481 mm required on the 0.4 mm CM5-style rows, 0.604 mm elsewhere). On the 0.65 mm rows the offsets go from (0.9, 1.6, 2.3) to (0.9, 1.73, 2.56) and the corridor to 0.604 mm; a 1.27 mm SOIC row is already wide and does not move. A pad whose deepened offset is rejected falls back to its neighbour's depth, where the corridor is 0.20 mm: decisively closed, and no knot there either. **A corridor is safe when it is comfortably open or decisively closed, never on the line.**

**2. The fanout ran before the pairs on every board.** D10's USB3 pair could not be laid at all: `pair_preroute` reported the section R20 to J_USB3 failing, and the debug map showed its corridor **start cell blocked**. What blocked it was C15's ground fanout via at (136.79, 86.48), 0.73 mm away. `prefanout.py` ran before `pair_preroute.py` in `full_a22.sh`, `full_b16.sh`, `full_c7.sh` and `full_d8.sh`, scattering plane vias across the board with no knowledge of the pair corridors, and the pre-router then had to thread the field it left. `prefanout.py` already reads existing tracks and vias as obstacles; the pre-router has no such freedom. The order is reversed in all four chains. **Measured on D the same afternoon: 4 of 5 pairs laid before, 5 of 5 after.**

**3. The fanout stub was sampled at two points.** With the pairs now on the board first, the reordered chain blocked on one `tracks_crossing`: a 3.375 mm GND fanout stub across the laid USB3_N leg. `prefanout.py` tested its stub at the midpoint and the three-quarter point only, which on a 3.4 mm stub leaves 1.1 mm between samples. It now samples every 0.2 mm, the way `escape.py` has since B16.

**4. A stub's A* was given one free cell at each end.** `stub_path` forced the start and goal cells passable and nothing else. Both ends of a stub lie on the net's **own** copper, so every neighbour of those cells is inside that copper's own clearance disc, the eight-neighbour loop finds nothing passable, and the search fails on its first step with a goal the map itself calls free. That is the shape of "no stub path at the via", which was 34 of B18's 66 pair failures. Each end now frees a 0.2 mm disc, which is same-net copper by construction. It did not close B18's `CARD1_CLK`: the printed start and goal maps show that pair's corridor ending in a pocket north-east of its via with a wall between, and the goal via in a three-cell channel running the other way. That one is congestion in the M.2 socket escape field, a placement question, not a search bug.

**And one gate that had never been armed.** `pour_stitch.py` was written on 8 September for D9's front ground pour (57 islands, eleven without a via, one of 222 mm2) and wired into **no finish script at all**. D10 ended its route with the B.Cu ground pour and the In1 plane reported open for exactly that reason. It now runs after `zone_pad_via.py` in the A23, B17, C8, D9 and P2 finishes. This is the fourth tool in the record written, tested and then left uncalled; the register class stands.

**A gate corrected rather than weakened.** The decoupling check failed C51, C53, C56 and C7 on "rail and ground pads reach a via or pour within 1.5 mm". Every ground pad passed, lying in the pour; every rail pad failed, because `+3V3_D8` and `+5V_D8` are **track** rails on D with no pour anywhere on the board. The question the test asks is whether a pad reaches its plane, and a rail carried by tracks has no plane to reach; its loop is the pad-to-pin distance, which the same check already measures (1.1 to 2.6 mm on all four). A net with no pour on the board is no longer asked a question that does not apply to it.

**The correction to the correction, and the first placement question answered by measurement.** Sampling the fanout stub every 0.2 mm with the full `clear()` predicate also tightened the other-net PAD rule, which keeps 0.5 mm of lane each side: 18 fanout vias were lost and ten fell through to the in-pad fallback, two of them landing 0.867 mm from C56's and C57's rail pads as clearance violations. The dense sample now tests **tracks only**, which is what the crossing needed; passing a pad is not the defect. With that, D's pre-route is **5 of 5 pairs laid and 0 hard of 15 types**. The pre-router's leg-crossing guard fired once on the way and rolled USB3 back rather than shipping a short, which is the behaviour it was written for.

Because the D pre-route chain runs in 47 seconds, where R20 and R21 go stopped being an argument and became a measurement. `gen_pcb_d3.py` takes `FIXED_OVERRIDE="R20=x,y,rot;R21=..."` for one run, and four candidates were swept: the placement as it stands (5 of 5 pairs, 0 hard), the pair moved into the north lane above the headphone amplifier (4 of 5, 0 hard), the same 2 mm higher (5 of 5, 6 hard: two courtyard overlaps and a short against the packed capacitor row), and the resistors rotated to exit north (5 of 5, 18 hard). **The placement as it stands wins and does not change.** Four minutes of box time replaced an hour of reasoning about a corridor, and the harness stays for the next placement question.

### 32.84 The display grew and nothing re-spaced the face around it (9 September 2026, 15:40 CEST; MESHSAT-862; owner question on render set eight)

The owner asked why the screen in `meshsat-1450-assembly-3-plate-off.png` is no longer level with the aluminium plate. It is not a render fault, and answering it found two collisions on the plate.

**Why it is proud.** Until set seven the face carried the Touch Display 2 as an **aperture**: `DISPLAY = dict(c=(0,-24), glass=(189.32,120.24), aperture=(169.35,100.51), pocket_depth=1.0, depth_below=7.0)`, a hole in the plate with 7.0 mm of body behind it and the lens about 1.1 mm proud, which reads flush. The 6 September device ruling replaced it with the **Xenarc 709GNK**, a sealed IP67 boxed monitor, 205.15 x 139.49 x **28.66 mm**, 1.2 kg, whose only mounting features are a VESA 50 pattern on its **back** and side holes at M4 x 6 mm maximum (`xenarc-709gnk-product-manual-v2.pdf`). It has no front flange to seal against a panel and its whole depth sits behind the glass, so it cannot be let into a 3 mm plate. The fit of 32.51 is therefore the box lying flat **on** the plate, four M4 up through the VESA pattern, with only its 57.85 x 43.12 mm connector block dropping through a 60 x 46 mm cutout into the backer's void and a gasket ring around that cutout doing the sealing. **28.66 mm proud is the design**, and it leaves 18 mm under the closed lid.

**What the swap did to the furniture.** The monitor is **15.83 mm wider and 19.25 mm taller** than the display it replaced, so its bottom edge moved **9.625 mm south**, from Y -84.120 to Y -93.745, and its top edge north to Y +45.745. Nothing re-spaced what sits around it, and two parts ended up underneath it:

| | its extent | monitor edge | overlap |
|---|---|---|---|
| e-paper lens (107.19 x 66.6 at Y 78) | Y 44.700 .. 111.300 | top +45.745 | **1.045 mm** over the lens' full 107.19 mm width |
| headset jack J_HSJ2 (16.0 mm hole at Y -101) | Y -109.0 .. -93.0 | bottom -93.745 | **0.745 mm** of the hole under the box |
| nameplate (76 x 26 laser marking at Y -101) | Y -114.0 .. -88.0 | bottom -93.745 | 5.745 mm of the marking hidden |

The first two are physical: the lens stands about 2 mm proud on its tape frame, so monitor and lens fight; and the box would have rested over an open 16 mm hole, which breaks the face seal the gasket ring is there to keep. Fixed by moving the e-paper centre Y 78 to 83 (gap to the monitor 3.955 mm, flex reach to J_EPD 28.2 mm of the 35.9 allowed), the headset jacks Y -101 to -104 (clear by 2.255 mm) and the nameplate Y -101 to -108 (clear by 1.255 mm, 3.75 mm from the plate edge). The bottom band between the monitor and the plate edge is **31.00 mm** and now holds the two jacks, the sounder, the battery bar and the nameplate, so that strip is full.

**The gate that was missing.** `panel1450.clearance_report()` answers a different question, a deep face part against a tall B16 part **under** the plate, and no check ever asked whether two things **on** the plate can both be there. `face_overlap_report()` compares every face item as its plan footprint with the collar its part needs, splits hardware from laser marking (marking has no height: it can only be hidden, and is reported rather than blocked), and `check_pcb_c.py` blocks on any hardware pair. The headset jacks carry their documented 16.0 mm hole and no nut collar, because the Amphenol Nexus drawing is still owed (32.50 item 9): their front hardware is the open question of that strip and is not guessed at in the gate.

**The lesson, which is the one the record keeps relearning:** a part swap is not finished when the new part fits its own site. The Xenarc was researched, dimensioned and placed correctly, and the two defects were in the parts nobody touched. A render caught what no gate did, and only because the owner read it.

### 32.85 The screen returns to the level of the plate (9 September 2026, 16:00 CEST; MESHSAT-862; owner ruling)

**Owner ruling, 15:55 CEST**, on being shown that the monitor stood 28.66 mm proud: *"i agreed to a better display BUT i never agreed that new display to violate the ruling of ALL displays surfaces MUST be on the same level as with the aluminium top board"*, and when asked how to pay for it: *"do all 3 (lower the stacks / re-do the cooling / change display) if required; the prerequisite is clear; the screen MUST be in the same surface level as the top aluminium board."* The ruling it enforces is **14.6** of 2 September 2026 21:50: *"the glass surface and the top shelf must be at the same level, the glass at most 0.5 to 0.8 mm proud"*, which had already superseded a design with the glass 9.46 mm proud. The Xenarc broke it by 28.66 mm for three days and no gate asked, because "proud" was prose in the record and a number in nobody's code.

**The front profile, read at last.** The record carried the 709GNK's outline (205.15 x 139.49 x 28.66) and nothing else. Rendering `xenarc-709gnk-dimensional-drawing-v3.pdf` at 400 dpi and reading its side view gives the shape the design needed all along: the body is **stepped**. A front bezel **flange 10.66 mm** thick carries the full outline, and behind it a smaller rear shell **18.00 mm** deep (10.66 + 18.00 = 28.66), its bottom face running 16.16 mm back before it curves away. The bezel opening is **173.15 x 117.55** (borders 16.0 either side, 11.0 top, 10.94 bottom) with the 153.6 x 90 active area inside it and the OSD keys in the bottom band. All of it is now in `XENARC`.

**The construction.** A 3 mm plate cannot pocket a 10.66 mm flange, so the plate carries a **full-body window, 205.75 x 140.09 R15** (body plus 0.3 mm a side). The monitor drops in from above until its **glass surface is level with the plate's top face**; the flange fills the plate's 3 mm and the rear shell hangs 25.66 mm into the void. A foam gasket seals the flange to the window land; a steel **rear frame** on four M4 at (+-110.875, +16 / -64) pulls the monitor up against it and carries the 1.2 kg, because the monitor's own VESA inserts take M4 x 6 mm maximum. The block cutout, the four VESA through holes and the gasket ring of 32.51 are withdrawn with the old construction.

**Making the 28.66 mm, measured not argued.** `tools/z_budget.py` prints the stack and the allocation; it exists because this depth had been argued in prose and never computed. The shortfall was **18.26 mm** against the 2.0 mm margin the C gate holds every deep face part to, and it came from three places:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| CM5 site envelope | one 30.0 mm box, cooler and fan together | heatsink **21.0 mm** over the whole site, fan **30.0 mm** as its own rectangle moved from cy 60 to **cy 63** (Y 48 to 78), clear of the monitor's edge at Y +45.745 by 2.255 mm |
| `B_TOP_Z` (B16's top copper) | 56.0 | **49.5**, the board drops 6.5 mm; the room was there, the tallest thing under B16 is D8's SA868 at Z 27.4 against B16's underside at 54.6 |
| PA flange (RA30H1317M1) | (-45, 20), dead centre of the footprint | **(-45, 70)**, same X, in the void's north band, 9.0 mm above the CM5 fans |
| backer notch | (42, -96, 105, -87), the connector block only | **(-104, -95, 104, -87)**, the body's full width; everything on that strip is south of it |

Result: the monitor's body bottom sits at Z 72.74 and the CM5 heatsinks top at 70.50, **+2.24 mm**. The no-vent ruling of 7 September keeps its fan per cooler; only the fan's position changed, which is the mildest form of "re-do the cooling" the owner authorised.

**The e-paper too, because the ruling says every display surface.** Its lens was 2.0 mm polycarbonate on a 0.4 mm VHB frame in a 1.0 mm pocket: 1.0 mm proud in the code and about 1.4 as built. It takes the C2 recipe of 14.6 instead, a **1.0 mm lens on 0.05 mm acrylic transfer tape** in the same pocket, ending **0.05 mm proud**. Foam anywhere in that joint breaks the limit.

**The gate.** `panel1450.proud_report()` returns every display surface over `PROUD_LIMIT` (0.8 mm, the figure of 14.6) and `check_pcb_c.py` blocks on it; `deep_parts()` gained the monitor body, so `clearance_report()` now judges the display against B16's tall parts exactly like every switch and jack. Both were silent before: a 28.66 mm violation of a standing ruling was found by the owner reading a render, not by the pipeline. That is the third time in two days a render caught what no gate did (32.83, 32.84, this), and each time the answer has been to write the number down where a gate can read it.

**Freed by the change:** the whole 46.5 mm between the plate and the closed lid over the display, where 17.84 mm stood before. The QMX lid tray's plan window was sized against the boxed monitor's east edge and no longer needs to be.

**Open items:** the rear frame is a new part and needs its drawing; the PA flange's harness length to D8 and the fan intake 9.0 mm below it want a check; and the window seal at a 3 mm land makes the monitor a bonded, serviceable-only-with-care part, which is the price of a 3 mm plate and a boxed monitor.

**Correction to 32.85, 9 September 2026 17:55 CEST.** The section says D's live `pour()` "never removed pour islands" and that P "had no island removal at all", and calls that D10's last open. That is wrong. `ISLAND_REMOVAL_MODE_ALWAYS` is **0**, which is KiCad's default: the token never reaches the board file (`grep -c island_removal_mode` on D10's board returns 0) and every zone on every board of this set has always removed its unconnected islands. The duplicate `pour()` in `gen_pcb_d3.py` was a real trap and deleting it stands; the setting was a no-op. D10's remaining open is a different fault and the numbers say so: the F.Cu ground pour has 58 filled areas and every one of them is connected to a pad, or the fill would have deleted it. Two of those areas are not connected **to each other**, which is what `pour_stitch.py` exists for, and it reports six stitched and thirteen left because a via at those points raised the hard count. That is the item to close, not the zone setting.

### 32.86 The I/O high-availability layer built, and the six defects building it exposed (9 September 2026, 18:45 CEST; MESHSAT-862; commits ab0e12f, 95ca54a, 280a3a1, efa081e, b22524e, 6e6cad7, b290c5b)

The architecture of `ARCH-PCB-B-IOHA.md` is now in the generators and **the whole B board builds with the gate at `RESULT: ALL PASS`**: 951 footprints, 840 nets, every placement region inside its rectangle, nothing unplaced. That is the pre-route state, not a route: no B deliverable is cut against this topology and B18 stays superseded.

Six defects came out of building it, and every one of them was found by reading data back rather than by inspecting the drawing.

**1. Two footprint keys were claims about a package that nobody had checked.** `Package_DFN_QFN:VQFN-20-1EP_2.5x4.5mm_P0.5mm_EP1.0x3.0mm` does not exist in any library, and `UQFN-10_1.4x1.8mm_P0.4mm` exists and is the wrong part: TI's RSE body is 1.5 x 2.0 mm at 0.5 mm pitch. The first stopped `gen_pcb_b3.py` at the netlist import, and because the chain carried on to the gate, **all 29 I/O HA invariants failed identically with an empty pad map**, which is exactly what a gate reading a board with no footprints on it looks like. Both land patterns are now generated from the manufacturer's own drawing (SLASEP7A 4222490/B and SCDS277C 4220307/A), as is the Skyworks changeover's (201132I Figure 12, including the ground land that merges with the exposed soldering area). This is the fourth time the record has caught a footprint key that was a claim; the rule stands and now has three more drawn examples.

**2. Reading that drawing found the pin table short.** SLASEP7A Table 5-1 gives GND on 5, **11** and 20 plus the exposed pad; the generator had 5 and 20 and no pad. Two pins of the part were floating.

**3. The rail defect, which made the whole ring decoration.** Each bank's hub, its 1.1 V core buck and both host-selection switches sat on `+3V3_S{s}B` and `+5V_S{s}`, and that 3.3 V buck is enabled by the module's own 3.3 V (`EN33_S{s}`, the divider on the CM5's rail). So slot 2 dying would have taken bank 2's hub with it, and moving the bank to a neighbour would have moved it to a dead hub. The plan of the morning said the hubs move to the device rail; the fabric was written and the rail tree was not read back. They are on `+3V3_DEV` and `+5V_DEV` now, hub reset pull-up, strap resistors and upstream VBUS sense included, and the 1.1 V core buck is fed from the device rail and always on. The PCIe switch and the NVMe socket stay on the slot rail deliberately: they are the module's. `check_pcb_b.py` refuses any part of a bank's path that carries that slot's rail, so it cannot come back.

**4. One band for the control plane was two mistakes.** A single rectangle across the module bay put back-side parts under the six CM5 receptacles, whose 0.4 mm rows escape into vias at the pad tips, and over the twelve M2.5 standoff holes at Y 36 and Y 84. It also put all three supervisors in one place, which is one failure domain again. They are in three separate pockets now: the gaps between the module columns at X -52 to -23 and 18 to 47, and the free underside of the QMX bay at X -158 to -129, clear of its four strap slots. The voters and the small logic sit in the band between the receptacles and the standoff row, Y 69 to 80.5.

**5. Each CAN fabric was terminated once, in the middle.** A bus terminated at one point reflects off both ends. Each fabric now carries a split termination (two 60R4 to a 4.7 nF) at controller A and another at controller C, which are its two physical ends after the pocket change.

**6. A stuck voter had no detection at all.** FMEA row 6 asked what notices a voter output frozen at one value, and nothing did. Each controller now reads the three bank selects and the WiFi select back on four spare inputs: no new parts, and a vote that does not match quorum is visible to the plane.

**Ruling 3 is built.** Slot 3's spare M-key drive socket is a second M.2 E-key 2230 carrying a second AW7915-AED, and the two cards share the existing pair of P2P antennas through two Skyworks SKY13351-378LF SPDT switches, one per chain, with three 22 pF DC blocks each because the data sheet requires every RF port blocked. Which card is live is the seventh voted bit and rests on the primary with the plane dark. The measured price on the primary path is 0.35 dB below 3 GHz and 0.50 dB from 3 to 6 GHz through the switch plus two U.FL transitions, so about 0.6 to 0.7 dB, not the 0.5 dB the ruling estimated.

**Stage 2 is closed** in `research-io-supervisor-2026-09-09.md`: the STM32H753 stands against the i.MX RT1180 on the owner's weighting with raw speed last, because the RT1180 has no internal flash (a new boot chip and a new single point per controller), is MAPBGA only at 0.8 mm, and has nothing buyable at the assembler, against 1465 of the pin-compatible H743VIT6. The board is drawn with the H753VI pin table and bought as the **H743VIT6, C114409**, the same die and pinout without the crypto accelerator that an I/O supervisor does not use. The FDCAN mapping is confirmed as PD0/PD1 and PB12/PB13 on AF9. **New for the blocked-vendor list: st.com refuses both the runner and the rented box** (connection refused, not a 403), so the mapping came from ST's own CubeMX-derived pin control file for this exact part number and the note says so.

**What it costs, measured against the netlist this work started from (756 parts at 096b67c, 925 now, +169: capacitors +69, resistors +52, ICs +33, transistors +5, LEDs +3, crystals +3, six U.FL, two removals):** 2,709 mm2 of part bounding box in five groups, all of it on the underside in pockets that carried nothing, about 0.9 W continuous, and a redistribution of about 0.8 A from the three slot rails onto `+5V_DEV`, which is an item for A22's next rail check and not a change in kit power. `+3V3_DEV` is a declared rail now (1.2 A against U25's 2 A part) so `dc_drop.py` judges it.
